challenges.title: Introduction to TypeScript: Why Types Matter
description: TypeScript is a strongly-typed superset of JavaScript developed by Microsoft. In 2026, TypeScript is the default choice for large-scale applications at companies like Microsoft, Google, Meta, Airbnb, and Stripe.
TypeScript adds static type checking — the ability to catch errors at compile-time (before running the code) rather than at runtime (when users encounter the bug).

// JavaScript - no type safety function add(a, b) { return a + b; } add('5', 3); // '53' - silent bug! // TypeScript - type safety function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } add('5', 3); // Error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'
TypeScript compiles to plain JavaScript, so it runs anywhere JS runs. The tsc compiler (TypeScript Compiler) strips type annotations and produces JS.
In these challenges, you'll write JavaScript that mimics TypeScript patterns — validating types at runtime as TypeScript would at compile time.
Instructions

Write a function typeSafeAdd that takes two parameters. If both are numbers, return their sum. If either is not a number, throw an Error with the message 'Both arguments must be numbers'. This mirrors what TypeScript's type checker enforces at compile time.
challengeSeed: // Mimics TypeScript: function add(a: number, b: number): number
function typeSafeAdd(a, b) {
// Validate types (TypeScript does this at compile time)
// Return sum if valid, throw Error if not
tests: var threw = false; try { typeSafeAdd('5', 3); } catch(e) { threw = true; } assert(threw, 'message: Should throw when a string is passed.');
var msg = ''; try { typeSafeAdd(1, null); } catch(e) { msg = e.message; } assert(msg === 'Both arguments must be numbers', 'message: Error message should be \'Both arguments must be numbers\'.');

challenges.title: TypeScript Interfaces: Defining Object Shapes
description: TypeScript interfaces define the shape of an object — what properties it must have and what their types are. They serve as a contract that objects must fulfill.

// TypeScript interface interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; role?: string; // optional property (the '?' means optional) } function greetUser(user: User): string { return `Hello, ${user.name}!`; } greetUser({ id: 1, name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' }); // OK greetUser({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }); // Error: missing 'email'
Interfaces can also define function signatures, array types, and can extend other interfaces (like class inheritance):
interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[]; }
In JavaScript, we validate interface compliance at runtime using type checking — useful for understanding how TypeScript's compile-time checks map to real logic.
Instructions

Write a function validateUser that takes an object and returns true if it conforms to a User interface (must have: id as a number, name as a string, email as a string), and false otherwise. The role property is optional.
challengeSeed: // Mimics TypeScript interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; role?: string; }
function validateUser(obj) {
// Check that obj has the correct properties with correct types
// id must be a number, name must be a string, email must be a string
// role is optional - if present, must be a string
tests: assert(validateUser({id: 1, name: 'Alice', email: 'a@b.com'}) === true, 'message: Valid user object should return true.');
assert(validateUser({id: 1, name: 'Alice', email: 'a@b.com', role: 'admin'}) === true, 'message: Valid user with optional role should return true.');
assert(validateUser({id: '1', name: 'Alice', email: 'a@b.com'}) === false, 'message: id as string should return false (TypeScript: number expected).');
assert(validateUser({name: 'Alice', email: 'a@b.com'}) === false, 'message: Missing required id should return false.');

challenges.title: TypeScript Generics: Writing Reusable Type-Safe Code
description: TypeScript generics allow you to write functions and classes that work with any type while maintaining type safety. The type is parameterized using angle brackets <T>.

// TypeScript generic function function identity<T>(arg: T): T { return arg; } identity<string>('hello'); // returns 'hello', type: string identity<number>(42); // returns 42, type: number // Generic array function function firstItem<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; } firstItem<string>(['a', 'b', 'c']); // 'a', typed as string firstItem<number>([1, 2, 3]); // 1, typed as number
Generics are used everywhere in TypeScript's standard library: Array<T>, Promise<T>, Map<K, V>, Set<T>.
In JavaScript, generics don't exist at runtime — but the equivalent pattern is writing functions that work regardless of type, which is how JavaScript has always worked.
Instructions
Write a function createStack that returns a stack data structure (push, pop, peek, isEmpty) that works with any type of value. This mirrors a generic Stack<T> class in TypeScript.
challengeSeed: // Mimics TypeScript: class Stack<T> { push(item: T): void; pop(): T; peek(): T; }
function createStack() {
var items = [];
return {
push: function(item) { /* add to top */ },
pop: function() { /* remove and return top item */ },
peek: function() { /* return top item without removing */ },
isEmpty: function() { /* return true if no items */ },
size: function() { /* return number of items */ }
tests: var s = createStack(); assert(s.isEmpty() === true, 'message: New stack should be empty.');
s.push(1); s.push(2); assert(s.peek() === 2, 'message: peek() should return the top item.');
assert(s.size() === 2, 'message: size() should return 2 after two pushes.');
assert(s.pop() === 2 && s.size() === 1, 'message: pop() should remove and return the top item.');

challenges.title: TypeScript Union Types and Type Guards
description: TypeScript union types allow a value to be one of several types, written with the | operator:

// Union type type StringOrNumber = string | number; function format(value: string | number): string { if (typeof value === 'string') { return value.toUpperCase(); // TypeScript knows it's a string here } return value.toFixed(2); // TypeScript knows it's a number here } format('hello'); // 'HELLO' format(3.14159); // '3.14'
The if (typeof value === 'string') check is called a type guard — it narrows the type within that block. TypeScript uses control flow analysis to track types through conditional branches.
Other type guards: instanceof checks, custom type guard functions with value is Type return types, and the in operator for checking property existence.
Instructions

Write a function formatValue that accepts a parameter which can be a string, number, boolean, or array. Return: the string uppercased, the number formatted with 2 decimal places, the boolean as 'yes' or 'no', and arrays as a comma-separated string.
challengeSeed: // TypeScript: function formatValue(val: string | number | boolean | any[]): string
function formatValue(val) {
// Use typeof and Array.isArray() as type guards
// Handle: string, number, boolean, array
tests: assert(formatValue(3.14159) === '3.14', 'message: Numbers should be formatted to 2 decimal places.');
assert(formatValue(true) === 'yes' && formatValue(false) === 'no', 'message: Booleans should return \'yes\' or \'no\'.');
assert(formatValue([1, 2, 3]) === '1, 2, 3', 'message: Arrays should be joined with \', \'.');

challenges.title: Async/Await and Promises in Modern JavaScript
description: Modern JavaScript (ES2017+, which TypeScript builds on) uses async/await for handling asynchronous operations. This is essential for working with APIs, databases, and AI services in 2026.

// TypeScript async function async function fetchUserData(userId: number): Promise<User> { const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`HTTP error: ${response.status}`); } const data: User = await response.json(); return data; } // Usage try { const user = await fetchUserData(42); console.log(user.name); } catch (error) { console.error('Failed to fetch user:', error); }
The Promise<T> generic type tells TypeScript what type the promise resolves to. async functions always return a Promise.
In 2026, async/await is used for: calling AI APIs (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini), fetching data from REST/GraphQL APIs, reading/writing files in Node.js, and database queries.
Instructions

Write an async function delay that takes a ms parameter and returns a Promise that resolves with the string 'done' after ms milliseconds. Then write runSequence that awaits two delay() calls and returns an array of their results.
challengeSeed: // TypeScript: function delay(ms: number): Promise<string>
function delay(ms) {
return new Promise(function(resolve) {
setTimeout(function() {
resolve('done');
// Write runSequence as async function using await
async function runSequence() {
// await delay(1), then await delay(1), return both results as an array
tests: assert(delay(1) instanceof Promise, 'message: delay() should return a Promise.');
delay(1).then(function(v) { assert(v === 'done', 'message: Promise should resolve with \'done\'.'); });
runSequence().then(function(arr) { assert(Array.isArray(arr) && arr.length === 2 && arr[0] === 'done' && arr[1] === 'done', 'message: runSequence should return an array of two \'done\' values.'); });
